newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Australian Broadcasting Corp Midday Update.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Australian Broadcasting Corp Midday Update.

text.p: HOWARD IN TOKYO
Australia's Ambassador to Japan says Japanese business leaders will show close interest in Prime Minister John Howard's speech to them tomorrow.
Ambassador Ashton Calvert says Japan's business leaders have a close interest in what the Howard Government is doing to reform the Australian economy.
He says they'll be listening closely to the speech Mr Howard will deliver tomorrow.
Today, Mr Howard will discuss trade, economic reform and the United States security alliance with key Japanese Government members in Tokyo.
BLACKHAWK INQUIRY BEGINS
In Perth, a Military Board of Inquiry has begun a three weeks hearing into a helicopter crash in Queensland that killed 18 soldiers.
Fifteen members of the elite Perth-based Special Air Service Regiment and three aircrew died in the crash, which occurred during training with Blackhawk helicopters near Townsville in June.
The Board of Inquiry is headed by four senior officers with expertise including aircraft engineering, special forces operations and helicopter instruction.

Counsel assisting, has told the hearing a wide range of issues will be investigated including preparation for the helicopter exercise, the conduct of soldiers and aircrew; and possible causes of the accident.
The Inquiry is first hearing evidence from the accident investigation team.
CALL FOR REVIEW OF MEDIA OWNERSHIP
A newspaper executive has called for a review of Australia's media ownership rules, saying foreign ownership restrictions are draconian.
Chief executive of Australian Provincial Newspapers, Cameron O'Reilly, says there are no foreign ownership restrictions in the
United Kingdom, South Africa, New Zealand, Canada and Ireland.
The Irish-based Independent Newspapers Group is a major shareholder in APN.
Mr O'Reilly told a business breakfast in Brisbane the media industry is no different from any other in that it requires investment and best practice.
EVANS CHALLENGES JOB BOOST
Federal Opposition Treasury spokesman, Gareth Evans, says the Government's industrial reforms will make unemployment worse, not better.
The Government is urging the Senate to pass its Workplace Relations Bill quickly, saying it'll help create jobs.
But Mr Evans says that's nonsense on stilts.
He says Treasurer Peter Costello concedes in his more honest moments that industrial relations legislation has nothing to do with unemployment reduction.
Mr Evans says the tough budget and slower economic growth will ensure unemployment worsens rather than improves.
BUILDING WORKERS END ACTION
The construction union says industrial action on building sites will cease by tomorrow morning.
The union has told the Industrial Relations Commission a majority of employers have agreed to make up income building workers have lost through the taxing of travel allowances.

The Master Builders' Association took the union to the Commission seeking fines under new bans clauses, to head off costly continuing strikes and bans on building sites in New South Wales and Victoria.
SALMONELLA VACCINE DEVELOPED
The risk of catching Salmonella-poisoning will be reduced, with a new vaccine for chickens and cattle that's being hailed as a major breakthrough.
The vaccine has been developed by scientists at Melbourne's RMIT.
It'll prevent the Salmonella bacterium infecting meat products and eggs, reducing the chance of it being transferred to people and causing gastro-enteritis.
The Head of biotechnology at the RMIT, Professor Peter Coloe says the vaccine is an important development for the food and animal industries because it will make food products safer.
-- Reuters Sydney Newsroom 61-2 373-1800
